title: Usability Testing Tools Comparison: Find the Right Fit
summary: 12 usability testing tools compared on test types, recruitment, AI analysis, security and September 2026 pricing, sorted by research maturity.
body_markdown:
This guide compares 12 usability testing tools: what each one tests, where participants come from, how analysis works, and what it costs as of September 2026.


Most teams pick a usability testing tool from a feature matrix, and six months later they're shopping for a replacement. Every tool on this list has enough features. The expensive mistake is picking one built for a different stage of research. What works for a two-person team running quick prototype tests doesn't hold up for an enterprise team running 30 studies a year with its own customers, its own security review and a growing group of PMs and designers running research.


So the tools below are grouped by the research maturity each one is built for, with a short note at the end on popular tools that sit next to usability testing but don't run tests.

## How we evaluated these tools


Every tool on this list was checked against the same five criteria, using each vendor's own product and pricing pages in September 2026.


**Supported test types.** Moderated sessions, unmoderated tasks, prototype tests and mobile testing. Some tools cover all of these; others do one well and leave the rest to another product.


**Recruitment.** Whether you can test with your own customers from your own CRM, a vendor panel, or both. For B2B teams this decides more than any feature list.


**Analysis and AI.** Transcription, AI summaries and themes, and whether findings from one study are searchable next to the others.


**Governance and security.** SSO, SOC 2, role-based permissions and consent management. These matter once people outside the research team start running studies.


**Pricing transparency.** Whether the vendor publishes a price, what the billing basis is (per seat, per session, per month or per year), and which features sit behind an enterprise contract.

## Before you compare tools: five questions that actually matter


Feature lists are distracting. Before you look at any tool, answer these:


**1. How structured is your research program?** Are you running ad hoc tests when someone asks, or do you have a quarterly research roadmap? Ad hoc teams need simplicity. Structured programs need scheduling,[panel management](https://www.greatquestion.com/blog/panel-management-guide) , and a[research repository](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/ux-research-repository-guide) that builds over time.


**2. Where do your participants come from?** If you're recruiting from your own customer base, you need a[research CRM](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/user-research-crm) and[screener surveys](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/screener-survey-guide) . If you're using third-party panels, you need a tool with panel integrations. This single question eliminates half the options for most teams.


**3. What research methods do you actually use?**[Usability tests](https://www.greatquestion.com/blog/true-user-intent-testing) ,[card sorting](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/card-sorting) ,[user interviews](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/user-interviews-guide) , surveys,[first-click testing](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/first-click-testing-guide) ,[preference tests](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/preference-testing-guide) ? If you use three or more methods regularly, a point solution for each one creates a Frankenstein of tools that costs more in context-switching than it saves in specialization.


**4. Is analysis a bottleneck?** If your team spends more time transcribing and synthesizing than actually running studies, your tool problem isn't methods. It's analysis. Look for[AI-powered analysis](https://www.greatquestion.com/features/ai) that can search, summarize, and surface themes across studies.


**5. What's your total research program cost?** Software is usually the smaller line in a research budget. People and participant costs are the larger ones. A tool that cuts analysis time can be worth more than a cheaper option, and if it helps you[recruit from your own customer base](https://www.greatquestion.com/features/research-recruitment) instead of buying panel sessions, that comes straight off your recruiting spend.

## For mature research operations


You're running 15-30+ research projects annually. You have dedicated researchers, and increasingly,[product managers and designers running their own studies](https://www.greatquestion.com/blog/people-who-do-research-our-favorite-term) too. Insights feed a number of teams. You need your usability testing tool to integrate with your customer data, scale across methods, and maintain governance as more people run research.


### 1. Great Question


Built for[product teams scaling research](https://www.greatquestion.com/) , not just researchers. Any PM or designer can launch a[usability test](https://www.greatquestion.com/features/unmoderated-prototype-testing) , run a[user interview](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/user-interviews-guide) , or send a survey without a research background, while research ops maintains controls over participant experience and data quality.


The platform handles[recruitment from your own CRM](https://www.greatquestion.com/features/research-recruitment) , so you're testing with real customers, not paid panelists.[AI-powered analysis](https://www.greatquestion.com/features/ai) searches, summarizes, and surfaces themes across every study. Scheduling, incentives, panel health tracking, consent management, and a[shared research repository](https://www.greatquestion.com/features/research-repository) are all built in. On[security](https://www.greatquestion.com/features/security) , Great Question has completed a SOC 2 Type II exam, is built to be GDPR compliant, and offers a BAA for research that touches PHI.


The structural difference: where other tools handle one part of research and leave you stitching together the rest, Great Question covers recruitment, methods, analysis, and repository in a single platform.[ServiceNow](https://www.greatquestion.com/customers/servicenow) cut recruitment time from 118 days to 6 days.[Sinch](https://www.greatquestion.com/customers/sinch) consolidated 8 tools and saved 35%, replacing UserTesting and Dovetail.[Procare Solutions](https://www.greatquestion.com/customers/procare-solutions) saves $15,000 a year after switching from UserTesting.


**Pricing (as of September 2026):** Self-serve is $129 per seat/month billed monthly, or $1,290 per seat/year billed annually, with a 14-day free trial. Enterprise is a custom annual plan. See[pricing](https://www.greatquestion.com/pricing) .


### 2. UserTesting


The enterprise incumbent. UserTesting's strength is its own participant network at scale, with a global panel across 60+ countries, which makes sense if you're running 100+ studies a year and need demographic breadth and SLAs. On 7 January 2026 UserTesting acquired User Interviews, the participant recruiting marketplace, and its Ultimate edition lists onboarding and managing custom audiences.


The structural difference for teams recruiting their own customers: UserTesting's platform and pricing are still organized around the panel, sold as test-based or team-based enterprise editions. If your research strategy depends on[testing with your own users](https://www.greatquestion.com/blog/a-guide-to-customer-research) from your own CRM, with consent, contact rules and participant history kept in one place, check how much of that lives in UserTesting itself and how much in a second product.


**Pricing (as of September 2026):** Advanced, Ultimate and Ultimate+ editions are all contact sales. No public prices.


### 3. Userlytics


A long-running testing platform for moderated and unmoderated studies across desktop, mobile apps and prototypes, with card sorting, tree testing and first-click tests alongside. Userlytics has its own participant panel and also lets you bring your own users, and its AI tools cover transcription, annotations, sentiment analysis and an AI UX report. It suits teams that buy research by the session, or agencies that need a private-label option. The pricing model is the thing to understand first: you're choosing between per-session project buys and an annual subscription for self-recruited testing.


**Pricing (as of September 2026):** Project Based is per session with no subscription (minimum 5 sessions). Premium, for bringing your own participants, is $699/month, paid annually. Limitless is a custom quote.


### 4. PlaybookUX


A mixed-methods platform with a built-in panel of 7M+ consumers and professionals. It covers unmoderated tests, moderated interviews, card sorts, tree tests, surveys, first-click, five-second and preference tests on computer, tablet and mobile. Its feature list also includes a participant CRM for your own users, repository features like tagging and search, Figma click testing and SSO. Panel sessions are priced per participant, so the total cost depends on how much you recruit through PlaybookUX. AI features are listed with the Enterprise plan.


**Pricing (as of September 2026):** Self-serve sign-up with pay-per-use panel credits (unmoderated panel participants from $65 each). Scale is $5,400/year and Pro is $8,800/year. Enterprise is contact sales.


## For teams running regular research


You're doing moderated interviews or unmoderated tests regularly. You have a research backlog. And you're discovering that the tool you started with wasn't built for everything you're actually doing now.


### 5. Maze


Strong at unmoderated prototype testing. Native Figma integration means you can go from prototype to test quickly, and running tests with 50+ participants is straightforward. Moderated interviews, AI-moderated interviews, mobile testing and the full AI feature set are now listed on the Enterprise plan, while Free and Starter cover one study a month. If your research program is expanding beyond "test this prototype" into the full[research lifecycle](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/ux-research-methods-guide) , including CRM-based recruiting from your own customers, check which plan you'd need.


**Pricing (as of September 2026):** Free plan (1 study/month, 5 seats). Starter is $99/month. Enterprise is custom pricing.


### 6. Lookback


Purpose-built for moderated remote research with video capture, timestamped notes, and observation rooms for stakeholders. It also runs unmoderated sessions. Recruitment is part of the plans now: each paid plan includes a set number of panel participants, you can bring your own participants for free, and extra panel recruits are pay as you go. Around the session, scheduling, participant tracking and analysis across studies are lighter than in a full research platform, so teams with a large program often pair Lookback with a CRM and a repository.


**Pricing (as of September 2026):** Freelance is $299/year (10 sessions, 1 panel participant). Team is $1,782/year and Insights Hub is $4,122/year. Pay-as-you-go panel participants are $49 each.


### 7. Loop11


An online usability testing tool focused on websites and prototypes, with moderated and unmoderated tests on desktop, mobile and tablet. Its reporting side is where it stands out: heatmaps, clickstreams, path analysis and UX benchmarking let you compare task success over time or against a competitor's site. Five-second and first-click tests, A/B tests and information architecture tests are included, along with AI insights and AI transcription. Participants are bring-your-own on the published plans, so you need your own recruiting source.


**Pricing (as of September 2026):** Rapid Insights is $179/month billed annually ($199 billed monthly) and includes 5 seats. Pro is $358/month billed annually. Enterprise is contact sales.


### 8. UXtweak


Broad method coverage for the price. UXtweak covers card sorting, tree testing, preference and five-second tests, surveys, first-click, prototype, website and mobile app testing, plus session recording. You can recruit from its User Panel, intercept visitors on your site, or use your own database. Live interviews and AI summaries, outlines and highlights are add-ons on the Business plan, and SSO, team management and legal or security assessments sit on the Custom plan. A good fit for small teams that want many methods without an enterprise contract.


**Pricing (as of September 2026):** Free plan (15 responses/month). Business is €92 per user license/month, billed annually. Custom is individual pricing.


### 9. Optimal Workshop


The information architecture specialist. If you need[card sorting](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/card-sorting) and tree testing, Optimal Workshop does those well, and its current plans also include prototype testing, live site testing and first-click testing, with AI-powered analytics and participant recruitment. Every plan has unlimited seats and all study types. The limit is study volume: Starter includes 5 launched studies a year, with more sold in bundles. Interviews are not part of the published plans, so you'll still need a separate tool and participant list for them.


**Pricing (as of September 2026):** Starter is $199/month, billed annually. Enterprise is custom pricing.


## For teams just starting out


You're running your first usability tests. Speed and simplicity matter more than depth. You need something that helps you validate designs without a steep learning curve.


### 10. Lyssna (formerly UsabilityHub)


Handles quick unmoderated tests:[preference tests](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/preference-testing-guide) , five-second tests, first-click tests and prototype walkthroughs, plus surveys and user interviews. Useful for fast design validation. The Growth plan adds AI follow-up questions and summaries, think-aloud recordings and live website testing, and caps in-depth studies at 5 a month. Responses from the Lyssna panel are priced separately on every plan. Participant management and a long-term research repository are thinner than in a dedicated research platform.


**Pricing (as of September 2026):** Free plan (3 seats, 15 self-recruited responses). Growth is $166/month billed annually ($199 billed monthly). Enterprise is talk to sales.


### 11. Useberry


Built around prototype testing. Import prototypes from Figma or ProtoPie and measure task completion, time on task and drop-offs, or test a live website. Useberry also runs live moderated interviews inside the product, with scheduling and calendar connections, and recruits from its own Participant Pool or through a shared study link. The Growth plan includes 300 responses and 5 interviews a month. AI features are marked as coming soon on Business and as an add-on on Enterprise, and SAML SSO starts on Business.


**Pricing (as of September 2026):** Free plan (10 responses/month). Growth is €83/month, billed yearly. Business is €659/month, billed yearly. Enterprise is contact sales.


### 12. UXArmy


A low-cost option for solo researchers and small teams. UXArmy runs unmoderated tests on prototypes, websites and mobile apps, moderated video sessions, surveys, card sorting, tree testing, first-click and preference tests. Plans run on monthly credits, with a participant panel as an add-on. The Organization plan adds an AI Moderator, participant management, SSO and centralized billing. It's a practical way to start testing on a small budget, with less depth in recruiting from your own customers and in governance.


**Pricing (as of September 2026):** Free plan (1 seat, 15 monthly credits). Starter is $25/month billed annually ($29 billed monthly). Pro is $82/month billed annually. Organization is custom pricing.


## Related tools that aren't usability testing tools


Two tools often show up in usability testing roundups but do a different job. They're worth knowing about, and they're not on the numbered list.


**Hotjar** is behavioral analytics: heatmaps, session replays and on-site surveys that show where users click, scroll and drop off on live pages. It can't run moderated sessions or task-based usability tests. Hotjar's pricing page now redirects to Contentsquare, which lists a Free plan and Growth from $39/month billed yearly ($49 billed monthly), as of September 2026.


**Dovetail** is a research repository. Teams use it to tag, theme and search qualitative data from interviews and usability sessions. It doesn't recruit participants or run tests, so it sits after your testing tool. As of September 2026 Dovetail lists a Free plan ($0 per user/month) and a custom-priced Enterprise plan.


## Point solutions vs. platforms: when to consolidate


Every tool in this comparison does something well in isolation. The real cost isn't any single tool's limitations. It's what happens when you have four or five of them stitched together.


The savings from consolidating are rarely about individual license costs. They come from less context-switching and training, one participant record instead of four, and findings that sit in one searchable place.


**Stick with point solutions if:** You run one research method, have a 2-3 person team, don't share participants across studies, and don't need insights to compound over time.


**Consolidate to a platform if:** You use a mix of[research methods](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/ux-research-methods-guide) , have 4+ people running studies, recruit from your own customer base, and need research findings that build on each other. Sinch consolidated 8 tools and saved 35%.


If you're managing a growing[B2B research program](https://www.greatquestion.com/blog/b2b-user-research-tips) , the consolidation question isn't "if" but "when."


## Six questions to ask before you buy


Once you've narrowed your shortlist, these questions reveal what demos hide:


**1. Can we import our participant list?** If the tool doesn't support CRM-based recruiting, you're dependent on their panels or manual workarounds. For[B2B teams researching their own customers](https://www.greatquestion.com/blog/a-guide-to-customer-research) , this is a dealbreaker.


**2. How does video work?** Auto-capture, shareable clips for stakeholders, searchable transcripts? Or do you need to record separately and upload?


**3. How accurate is transcription?** Low accuracy means you're manually correcting every interview. That's hours of work that compounds across studies.


**4. Can we get data out without a developer?** If insights are locked in the tool, you're renting analysis time. Export capabilities for your[research repository](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/ux-research-repository-guide) matter.


**5. Does it integrate with our stack?** Native CRM integration, Slack notifications, Jira ticket creation. Every manual handoff is a point where insights get lost.


**6. What if we leave?** Can you export your repository, videos, coded data, and participant history? The switching cost of losing years of research data is real.


## The bottom line


The best usability testing tool is the one your whole team actually uses, not just your researchers.


If you're just starting out: Lyssna, Useberry or UXArmy for quick unmoderated tests on a free or low-cost plan.


If you're running regular research and hitting tool limits: look hard at whether your current stack is creating more work than it saves.

## Frequently asked questions


What tools do UX researchers use?


Most UX researchers use a mix: a usability testing tool for moderated and unmoderated tests, a recruiting source (a vendor panel or their own customer list), a survey tool, and a[research repository](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/ux-research-repository-guide) for findings. Common testing tools include Great Question, UserTesting, Maze, Lyssna, Lookback, Optimal Workshop and UXtweak. Research teams at larger companies increasingly run all of this on one platform so participant data and findings stay in one place.


What is an example of usability testing?


A common example: you give five to eight participants a Figma prototype of a new checkout flow and ask each one to buy a specific item while thinking aloud. You record where they hesitate, what they misread and whether they finish the task, then fix the biggest problems before development. For a full walkthrough, see our[usability testing guide](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/usability-testing-guide) .


What is the best free usability testing tool?


It depends on what you want to test. As of September 2026, these tools publish a free plan on their own pricing pages: Maze (1 study a month, 5 seats, prototype testing and surveys), Lyssna (3 seats, 15 self-recruited responses), UXtweak (15 responses a month, 1 active study), Useberry (10 responses a month) and UXArmy (1 seat, 15 monthly credits). Free plans suit a first test or a proof of concept. Response caps and short result retention make them hard to run a program on.


Start cheap and upgrade later?


Most teams can't migrate participant databases, coded transcripts, and repository data without losing context. Pick the right tier for where you'll be in 12 months, not just where you are now.


Can't we just use Zoom?


You lose recruitment, scheduling, consent management, participant tracking, transcription, and searchable insights. All of that becomes manual work, and it grows with every additional study.


Can one tool replace the rest of the stack?


Yes. You won't beat Maze on unmoderated prototype speed, or Hotjar on behavioral analytics. But integration saves more than single-tool specialization when you're running a mix of methods, especially once you factor in the[research democratization](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/2025-democratization-report) trend where PMs and designers need self-serve access.
